newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan targets grain harvest recovery in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan targets grain harvest recovery in 1997.

text.p: Kazakhstan aims for a grain harvest of 14 million tonnes from its vast steppe lands this year, up from last year's disappointing 11.6 million, an agriculture ministry spokesman said on Tuesday.

"Weather conditions are normal, there is enough moisture in the soil...and this year we hope to gather around 16 million tonnes of grain bunker weight, or some 14 million tonnes cleaned weight," Alexander Korablin told Reuters.

Zhanybek Karibzhanov, Deputy Prime Minister in charge of agriculture policy, told a government meeting on Monday that the total sown area this year would be nearly the same as last year -- 19.4 million hectares, including 12.2 million to wheat.
The Central Asian state harvested a gross 13.2 million tonnes of grain last year, or a net 11.6 million.
Officials said bad weather, including a severe drought, were behind last year's result.
"Last year, crops were literally burnt by drought in west Kazakhstan and the northwest Aktyubinsk region," Korablin said.
A lack of machinery and spare parts, especially combine harvesters, was also to blame, and Korablin said the situation was little changed this year.
"We still have big problems -- a lack of machinery, fuel and lubricants," he said.
Karibzhanov said on Monday that farms owed 4.5 billion tenge to the country's oil producers and refineries for earlier deliveries of oil products.

President Nursultan Nazarbayev told the same government meeting that the state would pawn at local banks a total of one million tonnes of grain worth $160 million to enable farmers to get credits for necessary agricultural works.
Kazakhstan regularly harvested 25-28 million tonnes of grain in the Soviet era, but has struggled to keep up output in the face of cash and equipment shortages.
"We realise the quality is falling but, luckily, most of the buyers of Kazakh grain are not in the West but...mostly in the former Soviet Union," Korablin said.
Officials expect the former Soviet republic to export 5.6 million tonnes of grain this year, up 55 percent from last year.
